messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh is a 50-year-old Vietnamese American musician who came to treatment after years of living as if danger might step out from any doorway after dark. He had been divorced for some time and lived alone, supporting himself through club dates, wedding gigs, and teaching a few private students. The stalking began after a period of regular performances at the same small venues around the city. What he recalls clearly is the growing pattern before he understood it as a pattern: a man lingering too long by the stage after a set, then appearing again outside another venue across town, then waiting near Minh’s car after midnight load-outs. There were phone messages he deleted without saving, nights when he noticed someone standing across the street as he carried his keyboard to the trunk, and an unmistakable feeling of being studied. The most frightening encounters happened at night, after performances, when the streets were thinner and the pools of light between parked cars seemed too small. On one occasion he became aware that someone had followed him for several blocks after a gig; he remembers the sound of footsteps matching his pace, the metallic smell of damp pavement, the glare of headlights sliding over storefront glass, and the shock of turning and seeing the man closer than he had expected. Other parts of that period are simply gone. He can tell the story up to certain points and then loses it entirely, as though whole sections have been cut out.

That unevenness in his memory disturbs him almost as much as the stalking itself. He says there are parts he cannot recover no matter how hard he tries, especially around the most frightening nights when he was leaving venues alone. Yet fragments intrude without warning. While tuning his guitar or waiting for coffee, a piece of the memory can flash up and vanish—a shoulder near him in the dark, the scrape of a shoe, the reflection of someone watching from a window. At other times it is not a fragment but a total return. He is back there all at once: hearing steps behind him, feeling the night air on his skin, seeing the empty street and the shape of someone closing in. In those moments the memory does not feel like remembering. It feels present and complete, as if his senses have been pulled into that night again.

As the months went on, Minh came to believe that the people who should have protected him had failed him. He had expected that reporting what was happening would lead to some kind of safety or at least to being taken seriously. Instead, he was left with the feeling that he had been brushed aside, left to manage it alone, and that sense of institutional failure hardened into something bitter and isolating. He also began to judge himself harshly. He was ashamed of how frightened he had become and had come to believe that needing so much vigilance meant he was a weak person. He did not describe himself as angry so much as emptied out. He told the therapist that much of the time he felt dead inside, as though whatever part of him used to respond freely to music, people, or ordinary pleasure had gone flat.

His daily life narrowed around safety. Because he could not quickly assess danger in new environments, he stopped accepting work in unfamiliar clubs and turned down invitations to perform at venues he had never seen before, even when he needed the money. He preferred rooms where he already knew the exits, the staff, and the neighborhood outside. At gigs, especially evening ones, he found himself scanning the audience and entrances instead of settling into the set. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him: who kept looking over, who stayed after others left, who moved in his direction when he was packing up. Other musicians noticed he had become harder to talk to after shows. He left quickly, avoided lingering, and rarely joined anyone for a drink afterward. Night was always worse. He could get through the day with effort, but once the light faded he no longer felt safe. The walk to his car after a performance could consume his attention entirely, every passerby a possible threat.

By the time he sought help, the costs had become undeniable. His world had become smaller, his work more restricted, and his sense of himself meaner and more defeated. What finally brought him in was not one new incident but the recognition that he was still living in relation to the stalking long after it had ended, still choosing jobs, routes, and hours around fear. He said he was tired of feeling hollow and tired of measuring every room for danger before he could think about anything else. What frightened him most was the thought that this was permanent—that he had become a man who would never again feel safe at night, never again trust his own strength, and never again stand on a stage without also searching the room for who might be watching him.
